sentences.text: Sauroplites was a herbivorous ankylosaurian dinosaur that lived in China during the Early Cretaceous.
Its back was covered by oval osteoderms — bony plates embedded in the skin — with an asymmetric low keel reaching up to forty centimeters in length, while thirty-centimeter plates shielded its sides.
This animal is estimated to have been around six meters long.
The generic name Sauroplites means "saurian hoplite," derived from Greek words for lizard and armed foot soldier, while the specific name scutiger means "shield bearer" in Neo-Latin.
Fossil evidence suggests the carcass was deposited on its back, with the body armor largely articulated while other bones were eroded away.
The fossil was discovered in 1930 by Swedish paleontologist Anders Birger Bohlin near Tebch in Inner Mongolia during Sven Hedin's expeditions in Gansu province, China.
The type species Sauroplites scutiger was formally named and described by Bohlin in 1953.
The original specimens are lost and lack an inventory number, but casts exist at the American Museum of Natural History as specimen AMNH 2074.
While Bohlin originally placed Sauroplites in Ankylosauridae, a 2014 cladistic analysis by Arbour recovered it as a member of Nodosauridae based on its unique sacral shield.

The fossils were found in the Zhidan Group, dating from the Barremian to Aptian stages, placing Sauroplites in the middle of the Cretaceous period, approximately 125 to 112 million years ago, with a more precise estimate between 121.4 and 113.2 million years ago in what is now Asia.
Sauroplites was often considered a nomen dubium and some researchers believed it might actually belong to the genus Shamosaurus.
